messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mohammed, a 30-year-old Middle Eastern man divorced from his wife of ten years and working as a tax inspector in Los Angeles, has been grappling with the aftermath of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The accident occurred on a rainy night last year when he was driving home late after working overtime. A car, swerving due to slippery roads and possibly under the influence of alcohol, had collided head-on into his own vehicle. Mohammed vividly remembers the screeching tires, the sudden impact, and the smell of burning rubber and alcohol lingering in the air. Since then, certain triggers have become overwhelmingly potent for him. The crash imagery, the scent of alcohol, and even similar cars on the road can instantly plunge him back into that harrowing moment. Each time he encounters one of these triggers, his body reacts with a surge of adrenaline. For instance, when walking past a bar where patrons are exiting and carrying bottles of beer, Mohammed’s heart races as if the accident is happening again. These experiences have led to severe anxiety and hypervigilance; every unexpected sound or ordinary noise can startle him sharply. To cope with these intense reactions, Mohammed has adopted several maladaptive strategies. He spends long hours on his phone, playing games or browsing the internet, trying to avoid thinking about the accident at all costs. This constant digital escape not only occupies much of his free time but also leaves him feeling disconnected from reality and unable to engage in meaningful activities or relationships. The trauma has profoundly shaken Mohammed’s sense of self-worth and capability. He firmly believes that he can no longer rely on himself, doubting his ability to perform tasks that once defined him as a competent tax inspector. This loss of confidence extends into his personal life; he fears he will never be able to feel normal emotions again. These negative appraisals exacerbate his maladaptive behaviors—his undereating and reliance on digital distractions grow more pronounced, reflecting his deeper distrust in himself. His job as a tax inspector often requires driving to different locations for meetings with clients or other officials. However, the fear of encountering another vehicle accident makes Mohammed avoid driving altogether. This avoidance has practical consequences; he frequently cancels work-related travel plans and arranges teleconferences instead, which leads to increased stress from trying to coordinate remote arrangements and can create tension with his colleagues who depend on face-to-face interactions. Mohammed’s hypervigilance and startle response have also infiltrated his daily life. He is constantly on guard in public spaces like the office or restaurants, where unexpected noises trigger intense fear responses. This heightened state of alertness further reinforces his belief that he cannot trust himself to handle such situations, creating a vicious cycle. The more Mohammed engages in these maladaptive strategies and negative appraisals, the worse his symptoms become. He notices an increasing disconnect between him and his colleagues at work and friends from his past life. His undereating has led to significant weight loss and fatigue, which further diminishes his confidence and ability to function effectively. What finally brought Mohammed to seek help was a realization that he could no longer sustain this level of distress without intervention. The thought of never feeling normal again terrifies him the most, yet he also hopes for a return to a life where he can trust himself and engage fully with the world around him once more.
